[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]

== Biography ==
John was born in 1738. He was the son of [[Glasgow-2870|John Glasgow]] and [[Cranmer-656|Mary Cranmer]]. He passed away in 1792.

John Glasco/Glasgow was born in Glasgow, Scotland A prominent merchant in west Nottingham Township, York County, pennsylvania (Gibson's History of York County, Pennsylvania-Biography on son Congressman Hugh Glasgow)-married to Mary (Cranmer)-3-children-Sarah-Hugh-John. John Glasgow and wife Mary (Cranmer) Glasgow were buried in the Nottingham Old Presbyterian Buring Grounds in Rising Sun, Maryland. In 1960-All of the Bodies buried in the Old Presbyterian Burial Grounds were removed and reburied in a section of the West Nottingham Presbyterian Church Cemetery Cecil County, Maryland. This information comes from the History of The Nottingham Presbyterian Church now know as the West Nottingham Presbyterian Church and Cemetery.

== Research Notes ==
=== Current original-source review, 23 October 2026 ===

'''Original-page review, 23 October 2026:''' [https://ia903202.us.archive.org/BookReader/BookReaderImages.php?zip=/18/items/historyofyorkcou00gibs/historyofyorkcou00gibs_jp2.zip&file=historyofyorkcou00gibs_jp2/historyofyorkcou00gibs_0512.jp2&id=historyofyorkcou00gibs&scale=1&rotate=0 Gibson’s printed p. 414] gives Hugh’s exact 8 September 1769 Nottingham birth and says his unnamed father emigrated about 1730 and died at Nottingham in 1772. Hugh was the third son and the only one to reach adulthood. The page does '''not''' name John, Mary Cranmer, Sarah or the earlier sons; its storekeeper account concerns Hugh. Those names must not be attributed to this page. It is an original scan of a late 1886 compilation, not an original eighteenth-century birth or death entry. Its informant and independence from later family tradition are unknown.

The retained John-2871 remains the leading named father hypothesis for Hugh. The reviewed Chester tax index lists John with 80 acres in West Nottingham in 1787–1791 and Hugh with 80 acres in 1793–1799, after John’s recorded 1792 death. That consecutive name, locality and acreage pattern supports family succession, but the tax index is not a conveyance proving the same parcel or a father–son relationship. The newly inspected Gibson p. 414 names neither parent and instead says Hugh’s father emigrated about 1730 and died in 1772. Those dates conflict with John-2871’s retained 1738 birth and 1792 death. The late history may contain errors, so the existing father remains probable, but its general Nottingham context cannot be counted as independent agreement on this particular John. File 4225 independently documents a John’s 1792 East Nottingham estate; it does not name Hugh in the inspected surviving papers.

82% is an individual subjective estimate for Hugh-2873 → John-2871, reduced from 94% after original-page review. The index succession remains useful circumstantial evidence; the unnamed 1886 paternal account is substantive counterevidence. Neither John-2870 nor the 1789 shoemaker is selected as a replacement. No parent is detached, and no vital field or mother is changed.

The 1730/1772 account does not identify John-2870 either: child migration in 1730 would fit his 1722 baptism, but the retained May 1769 death conflicts with 1772. A September 1769 Hugh birth after a May death would permit posthumous fatherhood and is not an exclusion. No replacement father or mother follows.

Gibson’s inspected printed p. 414 explicitly calls Cunningham R. Glasgow the congressman Hugh Glasgow’s son and locates his farm about a mile south of the old Glasgow homestead, on the Maryland side of the Mason–Dixon line. The existing Cunningham Ramsay-3742, born 1806, is the adult son of that distinctive name in Hugh’s family. The other Cunningham, Sample-3747, died in infancy and cannot be the mature farmer described. The specific name, recorded father, adult generation and family locality identify the existing pair strongly beyond the earlier memorial/profile reconstruction.

97% is a confident identification of the existing father–child profile pair from an explicit son statement in a late compiled history. It is not a newly discovered birth entry. The book’s present-tense description may reflect information gathered before its 1886 publication; the profile’s retained 1885 death is not corrected to 1886. No mother, exact vital date, parent attachment or live WikiTree flag is changed.

'''Two original estates, not one John:''' [https://portal.laserfiche.com/Portal/DocView.aspx?id=772934&page=1065&repo=r-24f48cc6 file 4015], West Nottingham, contains an administration bond dated 31 March 1789, an inventory dated 26 March, and Peter Glasgow’s signed certificate of 26 March. Peter says the deceased John lived at his house about 27 years, was his uncle, and died intestate. Peter asks that John Taylor, '''Peter’s sister’s son''', administer. The bond appoints John Taylor; William Edmonston and Henry McCormick are securities, not kin established by their office. The inventory includes eleven old shoemaker lasts. The next estate begins at portal p. 1067. [https://glasgow.phenotype.dev/research/subjects/nottingham-probate/#john-shoemaker Complete connected family drafts and candidate review].

[https://portal.laserfiche.com/Portal/DocView.aspx?id=772936&page=247&repo=r-24f48cc6 File 4225], East Nottingham, has an inventory dated '''31 May 1792''', followed by its June oath. Portal p. 249 includes a debt against the estate of '''John Glasgow, shoemaker, deceased'''. The distinctive occupation, earlier death and nearby place make the 1789 uncle a probable identification of this deceased debtor; the debt does not prove the two Johns were related. The file’s replacement slip says the original administration bond is missing and directs the reader to '''Administration Book 2, p. 386'''. The next estate begins at portal p. 251. The surviving file does not supply a named Hugh heir.

John-2871, whose death is recorded in 1792, is a compatible candidate for the 1792 estate, with an East/West Nottingham locality question still open. The 1789 uncle cannot be assigned to John-2870 (retained death 1769) or John-2871 (1792) without resolving those actual conflicts. No generic name match, estate office or debt is converted into a father relationship. The inventory and bond dates are not exact death dates.

=== Earlier assessments retained as history ===
=== Individual father review, 22 October 2026 ===

The existing father [[Glasgow-2870]] is assessed at 17% (uncertain). The inherited Scottish pedigree gives John-2870 as the Pennsylvania John’s father. Its 1722/1738 dates would permit fatherhood at16 but are unverified, and the supposed Mary Cranmer mother is confused with the son’s wife in the same account. No migration or family record identifies the older John.

Uncertain17%; the American John’s real tax/cemetery history does not prove his Scottish parents. The young age is a caution, not an exclusion.

Next useful test: Resolve the Mary Cranmer generation and identify an actual migration or parent record.

Source basis already held: [https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-2871 WikiTree profile export for Glasgow-2871]. No new original inspected; no new father attached.


A possible identification concerns John Glasgow, Nottingham merchant and vendue attendee. John Glasgow signed a notice for a 2 September 1760 public vendue for creditors of deceased William Graham, including a 200-acre patent tract on the Susquehanna near Shepard's Ferry in Cecil County, Maryland; he also intended to open a store in Nottingham by the end of September.<ref>Pennsylvania Gazette, 14 August 1760, p.3, image 39404812; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/39404812/ record].</ref> The notice names no kin or origin. It does not establish Irish birth or migration. The identification remains uncertain.

=== Possible John Glascow, Chester County land and committee ===
John Glascow is an adjoining landholder in a West-Nottingham Township, Chester County execution-sale notice for 22½ acres, late Michael Dintz’s estate, bounded by Abraham Bunting, John Glascow and others.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/39401494/ The Pennsylvania Gazette, 1773-04-28, p.1].</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/39401765/ The Pennsylvania Gazette, 1773-05-05, p.5].</ref>

John Glascow is appointed to provide for distressed families of Associators in actual service by the Chester County Committee of Inspection and Observation, in a resolution dated 13 August 1776.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/39398635/ The Pennsylvania Gazette, 1776-08-28, p.3].</ref>

The adjoining-owner and committee appointments may concern one man but do not name his parents or wife. They require an active adult in 1773 and 1776; the John who died in May 1769 cannot be that living participant.

This may concern [[Glasgow-2871]]. Adult at the 1776 roster date and later located in Chester County, Pennsylvania. His listed parents are John Glasgow (Glasgow-2870) and Mary Cranmer; that father died in 1769, so the candidate is not excluded. No source ties this son to the 1776 appointment roster or establishes that his surname spelling was Glafcow.

=== Possible John Glasgow, Carlisle postal addressee, 1793 ===
John Glasgow, care of William Brown, Esq., is an addressee in the Carlisle post-office list headed 1 January 1793.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/1033763029/ The Carlisle Gazette, and the Western Repository of Knowledge, 1793-03-06, p.1].</ref>

"Care of William Brown, Esq." is the address qualification, not evidence of kinship. A postal entry alone does not establish that its addressee was alive on the list date.

This may concern [[Glasgow-2871]]. Pennsylvania regional/age comparison only. Exact 1792 death permits posthumous mail; no Carlisle or William Brown connection.

=== Possible John Glasgow, Kensing-/ton postal entry, 1769 ===
John Glasgow, Kensing- / ton, is an addressee in letters remaining at Philadelphia post office.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/39396485/ The Pennsylvania Gazette, 1769-10-26, p.1].</ref>

The place is printed over two lines as Kensing-/ton. The list does not establish a modern jurisdiction or family; it could include mail for a deceased addressee.

This may concern [[Glasgow-2871]]. Chronological/regional namesake; no identifying Kensing-/ton connection.

=== Possible John Glasgow, Nottingham/Chester postal and near-Oxford book records, 1758–1771 ===
John Glasgow, Nottingham, is an addressee in letters remaining at Philadelphia post office.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/39389283/ The Pennsylvania Gazette, 1758-01-12, p.1].</ref>

John Glasgow, in Nottingham Township, Chester County, is an addressee in letters remaining at Chester post office.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/1033731085/ The Pennsylvania Journal, or, Weekly Advertiser, 1765-10-17, p.1].</ref>

John Glasgow, Nottingham, is an addressee in letters remaining at Chester post office.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/39406491/ The Pennsylvania Gazette, 1765-11-28, p.4].</ref>

John Glasgow near Oxford is listed among people taking in subscriptions for De Jure Regni; advertisement dated 22 May 1766.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/39391550/ The Pennsylvania Gazette, 1766-05-29, p.4].</ref>

John Glasgow, in West Nottingham, Chester County, and William Glasgow are separate addressees in the Charles-Town, Maryland, post-office list headed 1 October 1771.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/41041559/ Maryland Gazette, 1771-10-24, p.3].</ref>

These entries form a qualified regional comparison, not a proved single life. A John who died in May 1769 could be the earlier collector/addressee; the 1771 letters could concern his surviving son, another man or posthumous mail. The separately listed William is not proved to be a relative.

This may concern [[Glasgow-2871]]. Compatible adult/Chester County namesake, especially for 1771 after the elder’s recorded 1769 death; no individual postal or book-agent connection.
